Renato, I have twenty minutes and then I have a patient. What do you need?
Twenty minutes is more than I need. One question: the new indication that was approved in March, have you started using it?
No, and I will tell you why. Nobody has shown me the safety data, and my waiting list is eight weeks long. I do not put a new protocol into a queue like that on somebody's word.
That is fair. So the barrier is evidence and time, not the product itself.
Exactly. And I will not endorse anything in front of the residents I train unless I have seen the data myself. My credibility with them is the only thing here that is really mine.
Then let me send the safety summary first, in a form you can show them. I am not asking you for anything today.
That is the first time somebody from the industry has said that to me this year. There is one more thing. I send patients to three colleagues in the east, and the referral stops there.
You want those clinics in the same support programme. I will map them and confirm whether they qualify, and I will come back to you either way.
Come back with the summary and the answer on the clinics, and I will find you thirty minutes instead of twenty.

I see representatives from the industry almost every week, and I can tell you in one minute whether I will see that person again. It has almost nothing to do with the product. The ones I trust are the ones who know what I actually treat. If somebody comes into my clinic and talks about an indication I have never worked with, I know they did not read anything about me before they came. The second thing is time. I have twenty minutes between consultations, and a representative who needs fifteen of them to arrive at the point is a representative I will not book again. Tell me what is new, tell me what changed since last time, and tell me what you want from me. The last one is the one nobody says out loud, and it is the one I respect most. And please do not ask me to endorse something in front of my residents before you have shown me the data. My credibility with them is the only thing in this room that is really mine.

For my first three years in this industry I treated every visit as a sale, and I was wrong in a way that took me a long time to see. I would prepare the message, deliver the message, and leave with a commitment that I wrote down and reported. The numbers looked fine. What I did not notice was that the doctors who mattered most had stopped telling me anything. They answered my questions and nothing else. A colleague who had been doing this for twenty years gave me one instruction. Go into the next four visits with no message at all, and come out with three things you did not know. It felt like wasting four visits. Two of them turned into the strongest advocacy I have ever had, because for the first time I understood what those doctors were actually trying to solve. A visit where you learn nothing is not a short visit. It is a visit you will have to repeat.

I visited Doctor Prado, who runs a private practice in the west of Sao Paulo. She is the strongest prescriber in the territory, but her advocacy has cooled since March. She asked for a written summary of the safety data that she can show to her residents. I committed to mapping the three clinics she refers her patients to.
